articles.body: Quem está começando em AWS conhece o medo de deixar alguma coisa ligada e descobrir no fim do mês que a fatura veio maior do que devia. Com agente de IA esse medo é ainda maior, porque não é óbvio o que está sendo cobrado enquanto o agente fica esperando alguém falar com ele. Em novembro a AWS colocou como padrão uma versão nova do AgentCore Runtime (o serviço da AWS onde os agentes de IA rodam), com uma promessa que chamou a minha atenção, a de que a memória que o agente libera deixa de ser cobrada. Para agentes que conversam em várias rodadas, a AWS fala em até 68% menos memória cobrada por sessão. articles.title: Diverting SQL injection attacks to an uncompressed image caused 37,000 requests and nearly 10 GB of outbound traffic
articles.excerpt: A developer spotted SQL injection probes in a client's access logs, rewrote matching requests to an uncompressed image for a laugh, and turned an automated scan into roughly 37,000 hits and nearly 10…
articles.body: Incident Overview and the Unoptimized Asset Bottleneck A developer spotted SQL injection probes in a client's access logs, rewrote matching requests to an uncompressed image for a laugh, and turned an automated scan into roughly 37,000 hits and nearly 10 GB of outbound traffic . That averages out to around 270 KB per response —a modest payload on a single visit, yet a heavy outbound drain when an automated loop fires tens of thousands of times before backing off. Serving an uncompressed image magnifies traffic spikes through byte-level inflation and repeated I/O. Uncompressed or lightly compressed raster data retains redundant pixel values and raw headers instead of collapsing repeating patterns into shorter bitstreams.
articles.author: Maxim Gerasimov

articles.title: How to Choose a Code Review AI Tool That Fits
articles.excerpt: Key takeaways Evaluate any code review AI tool by running it retroactively against 20-30 of your own past merge requests, including ones where a bug shipped. Treat a false-positive rate above roughly…
articles.body: Key takeaways Evaluate any code review AI tool by running it retroactively against 20-30 of your own past merge requests, including ones where a bug shipped. Treat a false-positive rate above roughly one in three as a trust-killer: once you skim past its comments, the tool has no value. Test GitLab integration against a nine-point checklist covering inline comments, re-review on pushes, approval gating, and self-hosted support. Pricing models diverge at scale: per-seat favors solo builders, per-token punishes large diffs, and per-repo punishes many side projects. Run a two-week pilot with week one in shadow mode and week two enforcing on one low-risk repo before adopting.

articles.title: Who turned the W upside down? Why Cassiopeia won't sit still
articles.excerpt: The queen in the northern night sky is supposedly one of the easiest constellations to recognize — you just look for a W. Or is that an M?
articles.body: Some constellations are like old friends. You know them well, they're always there, and they never seem to change. A case in point is Cassiopeia, the queen. Its beautiful name comes from Greek mythology — the mother of Andromeda — and its shape is said to represent a queen sitting on a throne. To a stargazer, Cassiopeia is best known as a prominent northern constellation shaped like the letter W. It's easy to find — look north, find five reasonably bright stars making a W, congratulate yourself on finding Cassiopeia and use it to get somewhere more interesting. It's so often a signpost, not a destination. But look north a few hours after dark this month, and you'll notice the W has gone.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 27, 1885: Astronomer captures 1st known photo of a meteor during an Andromedid meteor storm
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 27, 1885, an astronomer made the first known photograph of a meteor. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 27, 1885, an astronomer made the first known photograph of a meteor. The picture was taken by Austro-Hungarian astronomer Ladislaus Weinek. He captured the trail of the meteor on a photographic plate in the Czech Republic. The meteor he captured was part of the Andromedid meteor shower . The Andromedids were associated with Biela's Comet , which broke apart in the 1850s. When Weinek observed the meteor shower in 1885, it was in the middle of a meteor storm . This means that there were way more meteors than usual. Skywatchers could see thousands of meteors per hour. The November 1872 incidence of the Andromedid meteor shower, as seen over France, in a painting.
